rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.2-3.2 report own measurements (current, voltage, discharge, pressure every 10 min / 2 weeks at the Tarazona de La Mancha pumping station during the 2004 season) and a pumping-station model calibrated against these data; results report a 14% energy and 16% cost saving from changing the pump activation sequence.
rows.notes: The study concerns the energy efficiency and operating (energy) cost of a pumping station feeding an on-demand sprinkler network. It does not evaluate the investment cost of on-demand networks, nor compare on-demand with other delivery schedules, nor assess whether supply is guaranteed during peak periods. Its own result is that calibrated pump curves and a sequential activation of two variable-speed pumps reduce energy cost by about 16% (approx. 9,600 euro/season); it also derives the seasonal discharge distribution from electrical measurements. None of this bears on the claimed higher investment cost or peak-period supply guarantee, so Q2 is 'no'. Only Fig. 2/Table 3 give SD/CV for pump measurements, not for the claimed effect.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is a single-site case study (one pumping station, one irrigation season, 2004); the authors note results could vary with discharge distribution and pump working points, but this limitation concerns energy savings, not the cited claim.
